plot_extraction.response_text:
In a future industrial oligarchy, generations of the Vanderwater family rule factories and an enslaved, deliberately illiterate working class. A clandestine storyteller explains that the dynasty began with Bill Vange, a slave who betrayed his own people, crushed rebellions for the ruling class, and amassed great wealth. His children were eventually admitted into the master class and adopted the name Vanderwater.

Centuries later, workers at Roger Vanderwater’s textile factory, “Hell’s Bottom,” are exploited by overseers Joseph Clancy and Adolph Munster. The overseers steal a relief fund intended for sick and injured laborers and violently suppress complaints. After the workers petition Vanderwater, he sends their complaint back to the overseers, who have the workers beaten; the literate slave who wrote the petition is injured so badly that he begins dying.

When worker Tom Dixon loses an arm in a factory accident and is denied relief, the dying literate slave writes another petition. Disguised as a farm worker delivering Vanderwater’s prized strawberries, he enters the master’s palace and presents a tray containing the fruit, Dixon’s severed arm, and the petition clutched in its fingers. His courage forces Vanderwater to investigate. Finding the accusations true, Vanderwater brutally punishes the overseers and temporarily restores proper management of the workers’ fund.

The storyteller reveals that the brave, literate slave was his father, who secretly taught him to read before dying from his injuries. Although Vanderwater later offered him opportunities to rise within the system, he chose to become a wandering storyteller, secretly teaching slaves their history and urging them to learn to read so they can gain the knowledge and strength needed to abolish masters and slavery.

style_extraction.response_text:
The story adopts a layered pseudo-historical form, framing an orally transmitted workers’ tale between two scholarly editor’s notes from a remote future. The notes use formal, documentary language, precise dates, institutional references, and claims based on “internal evidences,” statute books, and court records. This apparatus gives the fiction the appearance of an authenticated historical fragment while creating dramatic irony: one future age coolly studies the brutal social order that an earlier future regarded as permanent. The contrast between archival detachment and the tale’s emotional immediacy is central to the style.

Within the frame, the dominant voice is that of a working-class storyteller addressing a live audience. His repeated vocative—“my brothers” or simply “brothers”—produces the cadence of a sermon, political speech, and clandestine lesson. He frequently speaks directly to his listeners, asks rhetorical questions, anticipates their ignorance, and relates unfamiliar events to their own experience: “You know yourselves what form such punishment takes.” The narration therefore feels communal rather than private. Its purpose is not merely to entertain but to educate, persuade, preserve suppressed history, and recruit the audience into literacy and resistance.

The diction combines plain, accessible storytelling with openly polemical language. Masters and institutions receive morally loaded descriptions such as “hell-hound,” “accursed,” “slave pens,” and “terrible industrial oligarchy,” while rebels are called “heroes” and “comrades.” Social relations are reduced to the stark vocabulary of “masters” and “slaves,” giving the story the clarity of a political parable. Even where the imagined system has its own laws and administrative arrangements, the language strips away their legitimacy and identifies industrial labour as slavery. Occasional archaic or elevated constructions—“wherein,” “thereafter,” “save to,” “had it not been,” and “whereon”—lend the oral tale a legendary, inherited quality.

The syntax is generally straightforward, cumulative, and highly repetitive. Important facts are reiterated in slightly altered forms, as in the changing names “Bill Vange,” “Sly Vange,” and “Bloody Vange,” or the insistence that the storyteller has read the truth “with my own eyes.” Repetition serves an oral mnemonic function while also intensifying the political argument. Short declarative sentences—“This is fact. I have read it with my own eyes in the records”—alternate with longer historical summaries and accumulative lists. Parenthetical interruptions, dashes, ellipses, and direct asides imitate the pauses and emphases of live speech.

The rhetoric is didactic and propagandistic in a deliberate rather than concealed way. The narrator repeatedly links literacy with knowledge, knowledge with strength, and strength with liberation. Historical exposition is shaped into moral instruction, and episodes are interpreted for the audience as they are told. Irony is often blunt and accusatory: workers possess rights “under the law,” but have no access to the law; Vanderwater’s minor headache is contrasted with Tom Dixon’s arm being torn from its socket; and a luxurious bedroom is called Paradise only to remind the audience that it was created by thousands of exploited lives. The storyteller’s questions—especially why one slave or the son of a slave should become master over others—invite a collective answer while making the desired conclusion unmistakable.

Structurally, the narrative delays its central incident through a long genealogy of the Vanderwater family. This digression establishes the ruling dynasty’s origins in betrayal and exposes class identity as historically manufactured rather than natural. The narrator then explicitly circles back—“I come back to the beginning of my tale”—and narrows the focus from centuries of oppression to one severed arm. The arm becomes the story’s governing symbol: an injured worker’s body is transformed into evidence, petition, accusation, and political spectacle. Its placement among blood-red strawberries creates the most vivid visual contrast in the story, opposing aristocratic delicacy and luxury to mutilated labour.

Violence is described plainly and concretely rather than through elaborate sensationalism. Beatings, executions, mutilations, and threatened punishments are presented as routine mechanisms of the social system. This matter-of-fact delivery makes the brutality feel institutional rather than exceptional. At the same time, the climactic tableau is strongly theatrical: the white arm against the red fruit, the petition clutched in dead fingers, the bleeding messenger surrounded by guards, and the master reading in silence. Colour contrast and physical stillness give the scene an emblematic, almost allegorical force.

Characterisation is economical and class-oriented. Individuals are defined chiefly by their place within the system and by the moral choices they make. The literate slave is never named, which allows him to represent an entire suppressed class, yet his courage, friendship, fatalism, and restrained speech make him personally affecting. Roger Vanderwater is neither rendered wholly benevolent nor allowed to escape responsibility. His eventual punishment of the overseers supplies temporary justice, but the narrator immediately qualifies it: the fund is managed properly only “for a time.” This prevents the episode from becoming a tale of salvation by a good master and redirects attention toward systemic change.

Dialogue is sparse, compressed, and aphoristic. The dying slave’s statement, “I have been sorry all my life that I was born,” condenses a lifetime of oppression into a single devastating reply. Such exchanges function less as naturalistic conversation than as memorable oral set pieces. They are designed to be repeated, retained, and passed from teller to listener.

The tone moves among scholarly detachment, indignation, grim irony, pathos, and revolutionary hope. The editor’s notes sound authoritative and retrospective; the storyteller sounds urgent, intimate, and morally certain. The ending reveals his personal connection to the central episode and turns family memory into political testimony. It closes not with narrative resolution but with an appeal to action, making the story itself an example of the “power in the printed word.” Overall, the style blends dystopian historiography, oral folklore, socialist sermon, martyr narrative, and political fable, using repetition, direct address, documentary framing, and stark symbolic imagery to make storytelling an instrument of resistance.

### EDITOR’S PRELIMINARY NOTE

The following narrative was discovered in the winter of 2841 among the uncatalogued wax-cylinder transcripts held by the Institute of Pre-Republican Industrial Studies at New Glasgow. The cylinder itself has perished, but a phonetic copy, made in 2713 by Assistant Archivist Lenore Hest, survives in Cabinet 44-B of the Workers’ Commonwealth Collection.

Internal evidences place the original recital between the years 2190 and 2210, during the later period of the North Atlantic Industrial Oligarchy. The speaker’s references to the Illiteracy Statutes, the household insignia of Roger Vanderwater, and the administration of factory relief funds agree substantially with court records of the period. His account of the punishment of the overseers Joseph Clancy and Adolph Munster is corroborated, though in guarded language, by the Vanderwater Domestic Chronicle for the year 2197.

The reader should remember that the words “worker” and “slave” were not legally interchangeable. The statute books described the factory population as “hereditary industrial dependents.” Nevertheless, these dependents could not leave their assigned districts, choose their employment, possess books, testify against masters, or educate their children. Their condition was therefore slavery, whatever name the law chose to give it.

The transcript begins after several introductory remarks which the early copyist judged inaudible.

---

Brothers, draw nearer.

Not so near that the sentry beyond the furnace wall may hear us, but near enough that I need not raise my voice. Feed the fire lightly. Smoke betrays a meeting almost as readily as a frightened man. And if any among you hears the iron heel of a patrolman on the stair, cough twice and overturn the little lamp.

There are twenty-three of us here tonight. I have counted you. Twenty-three men and women, and five children who pretend to sleep.

Let the children listen.

The masters say children should hear nothing save the factory bell, the overseer’s order, and the priest’s command to obey. Therefore let them hear everything.

I am going to tell you of an arm.

Yes, brothers, one arm—the arm of Tom Dixon, torn from his body in the looms of Hell’s Bottom. But before I tell you of the arm, I must tell you of the hand that built the Vanderwater throne. The masters begin their histories with their palaces. We begin ours beneath the foundations, among the bones.

You have heard the name Vanderwater. How could you not? It is stamped on the flour sacks, the machine belts, the marriage permits, and the brass tokens with which half this continent buys its bread. The Vanderwaters own mines in the west, grain plains in the south, steel furnaces beside the lakes, and textile pens along the old Atlantic rivers. Their red heron flies above prisons and schools alike. It flies above Hell’s Bottom.

Yet the first Vanderwater was not a Vanderwater.

His name was Bill Vange.

Do not look surprised. I have read this with my own eyes. Not heard it from a drunken carter, not learned it from an overseer’s joke, but read it in the old records, letter after letter, word after word. Bill Vange was a slave.

He was born in a machine district when the industrial masters were still tightening their chains upon the people. In those days the old liberties had not been wholly forgotten. Men remembered that their fathers had voted, spoken, travelled, and gathered without permits. Some could still read. Some possessed hidden books. Rebellion sprang up as grass springs through cracked stone.

Bill Vange was strong. He had broad shoulders and a smooth tongue, and at first the slaves trusted him. He carried messages between the machine wards. He knew where weapons were buried. He sat in councils with men whose names have been scraped from every public monument.

Then he sold them.

For a room above ground, for meat upon Sundays, for the right to strike men who had once called him comrade, Bill Vange betrayed the council. Thirty-seven rebels were taken in one night. Twelve were hanged from the crane towers. The remainder disappeared into the salt pits.

Thereafter the masters found Bill useful.

Whenever a factory rose, Bill went among the workers. He spoke their speech. He knew their signs. He could smell conspiracy as a kennel dog smells blood. At the Brackett Foundry he promised the rebels that the east gate would stand open. They rushed it and met cannon. At the Three Rivers Rising he advised the workers to gather in the square, where cavalry enclosed them. At Fallow Ridge he pointed out the hidden leaders one by one.

The slaves called him Sly Vange.

Later, when he commanded the punishment gangs, they called him Bloody Vange.

The masters called him William.

Remember that, brothers. A master may wash a traitor’s name more readily than a slave may wash soot from his hands.

Bill grew rich. Each rebellion he crushed brought him land, factories, or shares in the companies which owned the factory districts. Men and women who had been his companions were bought by him in batches. He worked them harder than the old masters worked theirs, for the new master is often the most merciless. He fears that mercy will reveal from whence he came.

But Bill could not enter the master class. The law still named him slave-born. He might dine with masters in private, hunt with them, lend money to them, and murder for them, yet their daughters would not dance with his sons.

So Bill served more eagerly.

His eldest son became a district captain. His second invented a punishment frame whereby six workers could be flogged at once. His daughter married the keeper of the Central Registry. In the third generation the family petitioned the Council of Proprietors. They presented lists of services rendered, rebellions suppressed, men executed, women transported, and profits increased.

The petition was granted.

The Vanges were admitted into the master class by Special Decree 88. They purchased an ancient title from a ruined house and altered their name. Vange became Vanderwater. Their slave blood vanished from the official genealogies. A painted ancestor in silver armour appeared upon the palace wall, though no such man had ever lived.

This, too, I have read.

And now the masters say the Vanderwaters were born to rule.

Born! Brothers, consider that word. What is this birth by which one infant comes into the world carrying a whip and another carrying chains? Does the master’s child emerge clothed in silk? Does the slave’s child have soot in its lungs before it breathes? Bill Vange was a slave. His grandchildren became masters because he betrayed enough slaves. That is the sacred beginning of the great Vanderwater house.

Why do I tell you this when I promised you an arm?

Because a tree is known by its roots, and because men who forget how masters were made may believe masters were made by God.

Now I come back to the beginning of my tale.

Roger Vanderwater, seventh of that name, owned Hell’s Bottom in the year of the Red Frost. Hell’s Bottom was a textile factory beside the black river, with seven spinning halls, four weaving halls, two dye houses, a dormitory for unmarried women, and slave pens for families. Its windows were high and narrow. Its roofs shut out daylight, save where the glass was broken in winter.

You know such places.

You know the air full of lint that enters the mouth and grows wet upon the tongue. You know the belts that run without rest, the iron teeth, the oil, the heat, and the floor trembling beneath bare feet. You know how a child may stand beside a machine at dawn and be carried out under a cloth before noon, while the machine loses no more than seven minutes.

Hell’s Bottom was governed by two overseers: Joseph Clancy and Adolph Munster.

Clancy was a lean man with white eyebrows and a voice like a file drawn across iron. Munster was swollen and red. He laughed while punishments were given. The workers called them the Needle and the Bladder, though not where either could hear.

By law—not justice, brothers, but law—a small part of the value produced at Hell’s Bottom was placed in a relief fund. When a worker was crushed, burned, blinded, or made sick by lint, the fund was supposed to provide food during recovery. Widows might receive bread for three months. Orphans under seven might receive milk.

These were rights under the law.

And what is a right to a slave who cannot read the law? It is a door painted upon a wall.

Clancy and Munster stole the fund. They entered false names in the account books and paid the money to themselves. Dead workers were shown as receiving relief for years. Children who had never existed consumed wagonloads of milk upon paper. Meanwhile the true injured starved in their pens.

When workers complained, Clancy said there was no money. When they complained again, Munster showed them the punishment room.

At last the workers prepared a petition to Roger Vanderwater.

This was dangerous. No slave might write without licence, and no gathering of more than six might discuss factory administration. Yet among the workers was one who could read and write.

I shall not tell you his name—not yet.

He had learned his letters from an old woman in the dye house. She traced them with a wet finger upon the black tables: A for air, B for bread, C for chain. When she died, he continued alone. He stole torn labels from freight boxes. He found newspapers used to wrap machine parts. At night he studied words while other men slept.

He wrote the petition.

It did not curse. It did not threaten. It spoke humbly, as slaves must speak when asking for a crumb of what they themselves have earned. It listed the sick, the maimed, and the widowed. It named the payments promised and the payments refused. Forty workers made their marks beneath it.

The petition went to Roger Vanderwater’s palace.

And what did Roger do?

He sent it back to Clancy and Munster.

Perhaps he did not read it. Perhaps he read two lines and felt bored. Perhaps the cream at breakfast was not warm enough. The motives of masters are recorded with great care when those motives excuse them. Their neglect is seldom recorded at all.

Clancy and Munster assembled the petitioners in the lower yard.

“You have complained of our management,” Clancy told them. “We shall improve your understanding of it.”

You know yourselves what form such improvement takes.

The forty were beaten. The old received fewer strokes because it was feared they might die too quickly; the strong received more. The literate slave who had written the words was punished worst of all. Munster wished to know where he had learned his letters. He would not say. They beat his back, broke two ribs, and crushed the fingers of his left hand.

He lived, but something within him had been injured past repair. After that day he coughed blood. He grew thinner. He still worked, for a dying slave is required to work until the hour in which he ceases to be profitable.

Weeks passed.

Then Tom Dixon lost his arm.

Tom worked in the third spinning hall. He was a quiet man, broad in the chest, with a wife and two small sons. One morning a belt began to slip from the upper wheel. Tom called for the line to be stopped. The floor captain refused because the day’s count was already behind.

Tom climbed the frame while it moved.

The belt caught his sleeve. His right arm went between belt and wheel. It did not cut cleanly. The machinery pulled at him, twisted him, and tore the arm from its socket. Only then was the line stopped.

They carried Tom to the factory surgeon. The surgeon burned the wound shut and ordered him returned to his pen. The severed arm was thrown upon a scrap cart.

Tom’s wife applied to the relief fund.

Clancy refused her.

“He injured himself by careless conduct,” said Clancy.

Tom lay white-faced upon a sack filled with straw. His children watched him shake. There was no meat, no medicine, and after three days no bread.

The literate slave visited him at night. He was near death himself. His breath rattled, and when he sat beside Tom, blood darkened his lips.

“Write again,” Tom’s wife begged.

“They will kill you,” Tom said.

The slave looked at him for a long time.

“I have been sorry all my life that I was born,” he replied. “I shall not be sorry to die if I can make them look.”

Those were his words. Remember them.

He wrote another petition with his unbroken hand.

This time he did not trust a guard, a clerk, or a messenger. He knew that words sent by the ordinary road return to slaves as blows. He decided to carry the words himself.

Now Roger Vanderwater possessed, among his many luxuries, a passion for strawberries. Not the small berries grown in common fields, but the great scarlet kind cultivated under glass in the southern farm district. His gardeners warmed the earth with buried pipes throughout the winter. Six workers tended the plants. Two others guarded them from birds. During the season, a tray was sent each morning from the glasshouse to the palace.

The literate slave learned the route.

Before dawn he stole a farm worker’s green coat. He took the empty silver tray from the cart shed and went to the refuse pit where Tom Dixon’s arm had been cast among greasy cloth and broken machine parts.

Brothers, he washed that arm.

Think of him at the black river in the hour before sunrise—a dying man kneeling in the mud, washing another slave’s severed arm. He cleaned the oil and lint from the skin. He closed the stiff fingers around the folded petition and bound them with thread so they would not open.

Then he entered the glasshouse.

He laid strawberries upon the tray, berry after berry, red and shining, until the silver could not be seen. In their midst he placed the arm.

The flesh was white from bloodlessness. The berries were red as the banners above the palace gate. The fingers clutched the paper.

Thus he set out for Paradise.

Yes, Paradise. That was the name Roger Vanderwater gave his palace. Its western bedrooms alone were larger than the family pens of Hell’s Bottom. Water leaped from marble basins. Birds from three continents sang beneath glass. The walls were covered with pictures, though slaves were punished for looking too long at them.

Paradise had been built by thousands who never entered it. Its carpets were woven by crooked children. Its silver came from men dying underground. Its baths were heated by coal carried on bleeding backs. Paradise was the sum of many hells.

At the service gate the guards saw a green farm coat and a tray of strawberries. They waved him through.

At the inner door a steward glanced beneath the cloth. He saw the upper layer of berries but not the arm. The slave was sent along the white corridor to the breakfast chamber.

Roger Vanderwater was in bed.

He had awakened with a headache.

This detail appears in the household record: “His lordship being indisposed by a pain of the head, breakfast was served in the east bedchamber.”

A pain of the head! The record preserves it. Tom Dixon’s arm is not mentioned.

Roger lay among blue cushions while a physician mixed scented water. His wife sat by the window reading a book. Books lay everywhere—upon tables, shelves, chairs—so plentiful that no one guarded them. What is forbidden to us is wasted upon them.

The slave entered carrying the covered tray.

The steward announced the morning strawberries.

Roger made an impatient gesture. “Set them down.”

The slave approached the bed.

His strength was failing. Blood had soaked through the back of the green coat where the old wounds had reopened. Two guards noticed it and moved toward him.

Before they could seize him, he pulled away the cloth.

No one spoke.

There were the strawberries, heaped like jewels. Across them lay Tom Dixon’s arm. The white hand rose from the red fruit, holding the petition as though the arm itself had travelled to accuse its owner’s master.

Roger Vanderwater stared.

His wife dropped her book.

The physician backed against the wall. One guard drew a pistol. The other seized the slave by the neck and forced him to his knees. Still the slave held the tray level. Not one berry fell.

“What is this?” Roger demanded.

“The morning account from Hell’s Bottom,” said the slave.

“Whose arm?”

“Tom Dixon’s.”

“Why is it here?”

“Because his petition could not come by itself.”

Roger looked at the paper in the dead fingers.

“Release him,” he said.

The guard obeyed.

Roger took the petition. He read it once. Then he read it again. The room was so still that the fountain in the courtyard could be heard through the glass.

“Are these charges true?”

The slave answered, “Come and count the empty bowls.”

Perhaps Roger saw then what no written word alone had forced him to see. Perhaps the arm upon his breakfast made Hell’s Bottom real to him for one minute. Masters often require the suffering of a thousand to be arranged as a spectacle before they will interrupt their comfort.

He ordered an investigation.

Clancy and Munster were summoned to Paradise that same day. They arrived in polished boots, believing they had been called to discuss production. They denied everything. The account books, they said, proved the relief fund had been properly administered.

But Roger had clerks who could read the lies better than slaves could. He sent agents to the pens. They found widows without bread, children without milk, and sick workers lying upon bare boards. They found false names, forged receipts, and money transferred into the overseers’ private accounts.

The charges were true.

Roger Vanderwater became furious.

Do not mistake the nature of his fury, brothers. It was not the theft from us that first enraged him. Clancy and Munster had stolen money bearing the Vanderwater seal. They had deceived a master. They had allowed disorder to reduce production. Worst of all, they had carried their corruption into his bedroom upon a silver tray.

Yet fury may sometimes fall in a useful direction.

Clancy was tied to the punishment frame he had employed upon the petitioners. Munster was compelled to administer the strokes. Then Munster was tied down, and Clancy, already bleeding, was made to strike him. When each had fallen, the palace guards continued.

Their property was seized. Their houses were emptied. Their families were expelled from the master quarter. Clancy was sent to the northern quarries. Munster went to the river-dredging gangs. Neither lived two years.

The relief fund was restored. A salaried clerk from the palace kept the books, and injured workers received payments.

For a time.

Remember those words: for a time.

Tom Dixon was given food and medicine. A light task was found for him in the packing room. His children received shoes. The workers said Roger Vanderwater had done justice.

Had he?

One thief had punished two smaller thieves. One master had corrected two servants who had damaged his property. Hell’s Bottom remained. The looms remained. The slave pens remained. Tom Dixon did not receive his arm again. No worker received freedom.

A good master is still a master, even when he loosens the chain one link.

And the literate slave?

Roger questioned him after the investigation. He was astonished that a factory worker could write so clearly. He offered him a place among the household clerks. Later, seeing that the man was dying, Roger promised that his son might be educated for service in the Vanderwater offices.

“You have intelligence,” Roger told him. “It should not be wasted among labourers.”

Do you hear the poison in that praise? Intelligence among slaves is called waste. Intelligence serving masters is called advancement.

The slave returned to Hell’s Bottom. He had no wish to die beneath the painted ancestors of Bloody Vange. His wounds had festered, and his lungs were failing. He lived through the winter, but only barely.

During those months he taught his son.

The boy was young. He came after the bell, sat beside his father’s straw bed, and learned letters scratched in soot upon a board. The father had only scraps: part of a freight list, three pages from a history, a hymn book with its cover torn away, and a punishment notice bearing the seal of Roger Vanderwater.

From these he taught everything he could.

A for arm.

B for bread.

C for chain.

He taught the boy to read the masters’ notices, then their account books, then their histories. He told him of Bill Vange, Sly Vange, Bloody Vange. He explained that the past had not vanished merely because the masters forbade slaves to know it.

“Words remember,” he said. “Men die. Words wait.”

In spring he could no longer rise. The boy asked whether he should accept Roger Vanderwater’s offer. He might enter the palace school. He might become a clerk. In time, if obedient, he might wear a clean coat and command other slaves.

His father answered slowly.

“If you climb by standing on your brothers, you have not escaped the pen. You have only become its gate.”

A few days later he died.

No monument bears his name. The factory register says only: “Male hand, number 7731, removed from roll—deceased.” The household chronicle calls him “the audacious petitioner.” The court record calls him “an unlicensed writer.”

I call him my father.

Yes, brothers. The man who carried Tom Dixon’s arm into Paradise was my father.

I was the boy who learned his letters in soot.

Roger Vanderwater did send for me. I entered the palace school for three months. I ate meat. I slept alone in a room with a window. They taught me figures so that I might count the labour of slaves and the profits of masters.

And I read.

I read more than they intended. I read the old decrees, the factory rolls, the trials of rebels, and the buried histories of the days before hereditary bondage. I found Bill Vange’s petition. I found the names of the thirty-seven he betrayed. I found proof of all my father had told me.

Then I fled.

I could have risen, they say. I could have become an office servant, a district clerk, perhaps even an overseer. Is that rising? If a slave is lifted high enough to hold the whip, does he cease to be a slave? Bill Vange thought so. His descendants still think so.

I chose another road.

I have walked through mine camps, furnace towns, grain districts, and weaving pens. I have told this tale in cellars, drains, abandoned shafts, and beneath the noise of engines. I have taught letters to children and old women. I have hidden pages inside flour barrels. I have copied names which the masters ordered forgotten.

That is why I came to you.

Not to tell you that Roger Vanderwater saved us. He did not.

Not to tell you that cruel overseers are the sole evil. Remove one Clancy and another will put on his boots. Drown one Munster and another will raise the punishment rod. The system breeds them as filth breeds flies.

I came to tell you that words are weapons.

Why do the masters forbid us to read? Is it because letters are delicate things, fit only for their soft hands? No. They fear what letters contain. A written law may be compared with a master’s action. An account may expose theft. A history may prove that what exists today did not always exist, and therefore need not exist tomorrow.

Knowledge gives memory.

Memory gives anger a direction.

Directed anger gives strength.

And strength, brothers, will end slavery.

Learn one letter tonight. Learn another tomorrow. Teach them to your children. Scratch them on walls, trace them in dust, stitch them beneath clothing. Read their laws. Read their ledgers. Read the names of the dead.

Some among you will be caught. Some will be beaten. I do not lie about the road. My father’s broken ribs are in every word I speak.

But remember the tray.

Remember the red strawberries and the white arm.

A severed arm could not work a loom. It could not lift a hammer or hold a child. Yet placed among the master’s luxuries, with a petition in its fingers, it became testimony. It entered where a living slave could scarcely enter. It forced the palace to look.

We must become such testimony—but living, joined together, and stronger than one man’s courage.

Alone, a hand is cut off.

Together, hands may tear down the gate.

The fire is low now. The watch will change before dawn. Go in pairs and leave by different streets. Let the children who pretended to sleep repeat tomorrow what they heard tonight.

And when you speak of my father, do not call him servant. Do not call him petitioner.

Call him comrade.

---

### EDITOR’S CONCLUDING NOTE

The identity of the narrator remains uncertain. Three persons arrested under the Education Suppression Act of 2204 claimed to be “the son of the Strawberry Petitioner,” possibly as an expression of solidarity rather than literal descent. A fourth, unnamed prisoner executed at Ironhaven in 2211, reportedly recited the phrase “Words remember; men die; words wait” immediately before death.

The relief regulations at Hell’s Bottom remained in force until 2202, when Roger Vanderwater’s successor transferred the fund into the general factory account. Surviving ledgers indicate that payments to injured workers then declined by approximately seventy-eight percent. Hell’s Bottom continued production until its destruction during the General Rising of 2236.

The Vanderwater estates were abolished by the First Commonwealth Decree of 2241. Excavations at the site of Paradise have uncovered portions of the eastern bedchamber, fragments of a silver serving tray, and the household archive from which several details in the foregoing narrative have been confirmed.

No record of Tom Dixon’s later life survives.

The name of the literate worker who carried his arm has not been recovered.

On the morning the sea returned the church bell, Mara Venn was repairing a clock that had not worked for thirty-seven years.

The clock belonged to Mr. Vale, the village postmaster, who had inherited it from an aunt he disliked and kept it out of obligation. It was a narrow thing of black wood, with a silver moon painted above the face. Every hour, the moon was supposed to turn from pale crescent to full and back again. It never did.

“Salt,” Mara said, holding up a corroded spring with her tweezers. “It gets into everything.”

Mr. Vale leaned on her counter. Beyond him, rain pressed against the windows of the shop.

“We’re three streets from the harbor.”

“Salt doesn’t care.”

As if to prove her point, a gust rattled the sign above the door: VENN & DAUGHTER, CLOCKS REPAIRED. The sign was older than Mara. There had been no Venn to stand beside her for eleven years, but she had never painted out the final two words.

Mr. Vale frowned at the clock’s scattered organs. “Can you fix it?”

“Of course.”

“You always say that.”

“And I am nearly always right.”

The door flew open before he could answer. Tomas Reed stood on the threshold, drenched to the skin, his red scarf hanging like a wounded flag.

“They found it,” he said.

Mara looked down at the tiny spring in her tweezers. “Found what?”

“The bell.”

Behind him, thunder rolled over the sea.

Everyone in Bellweather knew the story.

A hundred and nine years earlier, before the stone harbor wall and the lighthouse and the white hotels on the cliffs, the village church had stood on a hill above the eastern shore. During the Great Storm, the hill collapsed. The church went into the sea with twenty-three people sheltering inside it.

The bodies were recovered over the following weeks, but the bell was not.

Fishermen claimed they could hear it beneath their boats before bad weather. Children dared one another to swim over the drowned hill at midnight. Old Mrs. Cale insisted it rang on the night her husband died, although old Mrs. Cale also insisted she had once danced with a prince of Spain.

Mara did not believe in stories that could not be opened with a screwdriver.

She placed the spring on a square of blue cloth.

“Where?”

“North beach,” Tomas said. “The storm uncovered something in the rocks. Half the village is there.”

“The sensible half?”

“The curious half.”

Mr. Vale straightened. “I ought to see this.”

“You ought to deliver the post,” Mara said.

“History can’t wait for the afternoon collection.”

Apparently, neither could he. He pulled up his collar and hurried out. Tomas remained in the doorway, dripping steadily.

“You’re coming,” he said.

It was not a question.

“I have work.”

“You have one customer, and he just left.”

“I have twelve clocks waiting.”

“They’ve waited this long.”

Mara glanced at the shelves behind her. Clocks stood in solemn rows: brass carriage clocks, painted kitchen clocks, a walnut grandfather clock whose hands had stopped at twenty past three. For years she had repaired the village’s hours. She polished wheels, replaced pins, adjusted pendulums, and returned time to people who complained it had been running fast or slow.

Time, she knew, did neither. People did.

Tomas was still waiting.

He had been waiting for Mara in one way or another since they were children: outside school, at the end of the harbor wall, beneath her upstairs window on summer nights. He was patient only with her. With everything else, he rushed.

She took her oilskin coat from its hook.

“If this is an anchor,” she said, “I’m charging you for the afternoon.”

North beach lay beyond the lighthouse, where the cliffs bent inward and trapped whatever the sea no longer wanted. Driftwood, bottles, fishing nets, and once, when Mara was nine, a crate of oranges had washed ashore there.

That morning, the entire beach smelled of iron and torn weeds.

Villagers crowded among the rocks. Some carried umbrellas. Most had forgotten them. Children climbed wherever adults told them not to climb. The mayor stood on a boulder, shouting instructions nobody obeyed.

At the center of the crowd was a bell.

It lay on its side in a bed of black seaweed. Green with age, cracked along the lip, it was larger than Mara had imagined. Faded letters circled its crown.

Tomas pushed through the crowd, making a path for her.

“There,” he said, as proudly as if he had raised it himself.

Several men had tied ropes around the bell. Every time a wave entered the cove, water foamed around its mouth, and the bell seemed to breathe.

Mara crouched beside it. Barnacles covered the bronze. She brushed weed from the inscription.

WE CALL THE LOST—

The rest was hidden beneath the rock.

“Don’t touch it,” said a voice behind her.

Elias Venn had grown old without permission.

Mara remembered him as a wide-shouldered man who could carry a longcase clock alone. The man on the beach leaned on an ash cane. His white hair had escaped from beneath his cap, and rain clung to his beard.

“Uncle,” Mara said.

He looked at the bell, not at her. “It should have stayed down.”

“You don’t believe the old stories.”

“I believe the sea buries things for a reason.”

Tomas gave Mara a quick glance. Family disagreements in Bellweather had the awkward quality of public performances. There were always spectators, and everyone knew the opening lines.

Mara stood. “Did you come all this way to tell the sea it made a mistake?”

“I came to stop fools from ringing it.”

The mayor, who had been supervising the ropes, laughed too loudly. “It’s cracked, Elias. It couldn’t ring if the saints themselves pulled the rope.”

Elias’s expression did not change. “Then you’ve nothing to prove.”

A stronger wave broke against the rocks. The bell shifted.

From somewhere inside it came a low metallic sound.

Not a ring. Not quite.

The crowd fell silent.

Mara felt the note in her ribs.

Then a child squealed, someone laughed, and the moment broke into a dozen explanations. A loose stone. The chains. The water. An echo from the harbor.

Elias turned away.

As he passed Mara, he said quietly, “Your father heard it too.”

She caught his arm.

He stopped but did not look at her.

“My father heard what?”

Another wave washed around their boots.

Elias pulled free. “Ask the bell.”

By noon, the villagers had dragged it above the tide line. By two, it stood in the market square on a timber frame borrowed from the boatyard. Someone scrubbed away the weeds. Someone else sold hot cider. The mayor proposed a festival.

Bellweather had always been efficient at turning tragedy into tourism.

Mara returned to her shop and locked the door.

She told herself she had come back for dry clothes, but instead she climbed the narrow stairs to the attic. The room smelled of dust, cedar, and machine oil. Her father’s workbench still stood beneath the round window. She had not touched it since the winter he disappeared.

Jonas Venn had left his coat on the peg, his supper on the table, and a half-repaired watch in the vise. No one had seen him go. Three days later, Tomas found one of his boots on the eastern shore.

The sea did not return the rest of him.

Mara knelt before the chest under the bench. Inside were account books, old tools, and bundles of papers tied with string. Her father’s handwriting filled page after page: neat columns, quick sketches of escapements, notes on customers.

She found the bell in the seventh book.

At first it was only a drawing in the margin: a cracked bronze shape, the letters around its crown carefully copied.

WE CALL THE LOST HOME.

Beneath it, Jonas had written:

Elias says it is imagination. But the sound is real. Three nights now, always at 1:17. Not from the sea—from inside the clocks.

Mara read the line twice.

The next pages were crowded with observations.

Pendulums stopping at 1:17.

Watches running backward.

A tide chart.

A map of the old church hill.

Then, on the final written page:

A bell does not create time. It divides it. Before and after. Here and gone. If the drowned bell rings, perhaps the division weakens.

Below that, in darker ink:

I heard Clara.

Mara closed the book.

Clara was her mother.

She had died when Mara was six, after three days of fever. Mara remembered cool fingers against her forehead, a blue ribbon, and a song with no ending.

Downstairs, a clock struck four. Another followed, then another, until the shop filled with overlapping chimes.

Behind them, very faintly, Mara heard a woman singing.

She stood so quickly that the book fell.

The song continued for no more than a breath. Four descending notes.

Mara knew them.

She had spent years pretending she did not.

At sunset, Elias was waiting outside the shop.

“You should have told me,” Mara said.

He looked toward the windows, where dozens of clock faces shone in the fading light. “Would you have believed me?”

“No.”

“That was my hope.”

She unlocked the door and let him in. Neither removed a coat. Rain ticked against the glass, soft and regular.

Elias walked to the counter. The postmaster’s black clock lay open where Mara had left it.

“Jonas came to me a month before he vanished,” he said. “He said the clocks were speaking. I thought grief had finally broken him. Your mother’s death left a door open in him, and he spent years waiting for something to come through.”

“He wrote that he heard her.”

“So did I.”

Mara stared at him.

“Once,” Elias said. “In this room. Every clock stopped, and Clara said my name. Just my name. Jonas took it as proof. I took it as warning.”

“Warning of what?”

“That the dead might call us as easily as we call them.”

In the square, a hammer struck wood. Men were reinforcing the frame for the bell.

Mara opened her father’s notebook on the counter. “He went to the eastern shore at 1:17.”

“Yes.”

“You knew?”

“I guessed. By the time I reached the beach, he was gone.”

“And you never thought to tell his daughter?”

“You were nineteen. You had just lost the only parent you had left.”

“I lost him every day for eleven years.”

Elias flinched.

Mara had wanted to hurt him. The knowledge brought no satisfaction.

Outside, the rain stopped. In the sudden quiet, they heard footsteps approaching. Tomas entered without knocking.

“They’re going to ring it at midnight,” he said.

Elias swore.

“The mayor says it opens the Founders’ Festival.”

“The founders have been dead for two centuries,” Mara said. “Surely they don’t mind waiting until morning.”

Tomas’s face was pale. “There’s more. Since they raised the bell, people have been hearing things. Mr. Vale heard his aunt in the post office. Mrs. Cale heard her husband singing in the chimney. Half the clocks in the inn have stopped.”

“At what time?” Elias asked.

“Seventeen past one.”

The three of them looked at the clock on the wall.

It was five minutes to midnight.

The square glittered with lanterns.

Nearly everyone in Bellweather had gathered there, drawn by fear, excitement, or the certainty that anything supernatural should happen in front of witnesses. The bell hung from a new iron bar. A rope had been looped through its rusted clapper.

The mayor climbed onto a platform.

Mara, Elias, and Tomas pushed into the crowd.

“You cannot ring it,” Elias called.

The mayor raised both hands. “Friends, this bell is part of our heritage.”

“So is cholera,” Mara said. “We don’t hold a festival for that.”

A few people laughed.

The mayor did not. “Miss Venn, I respect your skill with clocks, but this is a civic matter.”

“It is a timepiece.”

“It’s a bell.”

“What do you think bells are for?”

The clockmaker’s argument caused a murmur. Bellweather respected expertise, particularly when it was expressed irritably.

Mara climbed onto the platform.

“My father studied this bell before he disappeared,” she said. “Many of you have heard voices tonight. People you loved. People you lost. If the bell has caused that without being rung, we cannot know what will happen when it sounds.”

Mr. Vale removed his hat. Mrs. Cale began to cry.

The mayor lowered his voice. “Are you asking me to cancel the first interesting event this village has had in years because of ghosts?”

“Yes.”

The harbor clock began to strike midnight.

On the first note, every lantern in the square went out.

Darkness swept over them.

Someone screamed.

Then the drowned bell rang.

No one had pulled the rope.

Its cracked voice rolled through the square, deeper than thunder. Mara felt the ground tilt beneath her. Shop windows burst outward. Birds rose shrieking from the roofs.

The bell rang again.

The square changed.

For an instant, another village stood within Bellweather: cottages with thatched roofs, muddy lanes, the old church on its green hill. Pale figures crowded the streets. Water streamed from their clothes. Seaweed twisted in their hair.

Then the vision vanished.

People cried out names.

Loved ones appeared between raindrops, in windows, beneath archways. A dead brother lifted his hand. A lost child ran toward her mother. Sailors drowned decades apart stood together beside the fountain, staring at the sky.

Mara heard the unfinished song.

Her mother stood at the far end of the square, wearing the gray dress in which she had been buried. Beside her was Jonas.

He looked exactly as he had on the final morning: brown hair untidy, spectacles low on his nose, waistcoat missing a button.

“Mara,” he said.

The crowd disappeared from her awareness. The square narrowed to the distance between them.

She stepped off the platform.

“Mara,” Elias warned.

Jonas smiled. “Little wren.”

No one had called her that since he vanished.

She crossed half the square before Tomas caught her wrist.

“Wait.”

She tried to pull free.

Her father’s smile trembled. Behind him, the street darkened, not with night but with depth. Water seemed to stand upright like a wall.

“Come home,” he said.

The words were gentle.

Around Mara, others were moving toward their dead. Mrs. Cale reached for her husband. The baker walked toward two small figures holding hands. A fisherman embraced the wet shadow of his brother—and both vanished.

The bell swung.

It would ring a third time.

Mara looked at the harbor clock. Its hands spun backward, gathering speed. Eleven fifty. Eleven thirty. Ten. Nine.

Roofs flickered between tile and thatch. The market fountain became an ancient well. If the clock continued, Bellweather would be dragged into the hour the church drowned.

“A bell divides time,” Mara whispered.

Tomas tightened his grip. “What?”

“My father’s notebook. Before and after. Here and gone.”

“How does that help us?”

She looked at the cracked bell, then at the clocks visible through the broken windows of her shop. All showed 1:17.

Clocks did not command time. They agreed upon it.

“Elias!” she shouted. “The bell is pulling everything toward one moment. We have to give the village another.”

Her uncle understood first. He seized the mayor’s ceremonial hammer and struck the little brass clock mounted above the town hall door.

Once.

The sound was thin against the drowned bell’s roar, but it was clear.

Mara ran to her shop.

Tomas followed, dragging her past the pale figure of Jonas. Her father reached for her.

“Little wren.”

She stopped.

For eleven years, she had imagined what she would say if he returned. She had prepared accusations, pleas, forgiveness. Now, seeing the sea behind his eyes, she understood that whatever wore his face held only the part of him that had wanted to come home.

That part was real.

It was simply not all of him.

“I waited for you,” she said.

“I know.”

“I cannot keep waiting.”

His expression softened.

Then Tomas pulled her through the shop door.

Mara seized the first clock she reached, wound it, and set the hands to midnight. Tomas took another. Elias appeared carrying three from the town hall.

“Midnight?” he asked.

“Midnight,” Mara said. “A new day. Make them agree.”

Word spread through the square.

People stumbled into houses and returned with clocks. Mantel clocks, watches, alarm clocks, kitchen clocks shaped like cats. They set every hand to twelve. Those who could not reach their homes rang bicycle bells, struck pans, blew whistles.

The drowned bell began its third swing.

Mara placed Mr. Vale’s black clock on the counter. The corroded spring still lay on the blue cloth.

“Can you fix it?” Tomas asked.

“Of course.”

She fitted the spring, closed the mechanism, and turned the key.

The silver moon above the face moved.

Outside, the drowned bell’s clapper rose.

“Now!” Mara shouted.

Bellweather rang.

A hundred clocks struck midnight. Watches chimed. Pans crashed. The harbor horn bellowed. People shouted the hour until their voices broke.

The sound met the bell’s third note in the air.

For one impossible moment, the village stood between two times.

Mara saw the church hill beneath the sea. She saw twenty-three frightened people gathered in the nave. She saw Jonas on the shore eleven years earlier, walking into black water while Clara’s song drifted over the waves.

Then she saw him turn.

Not the ghost in the square. Her father as he had truly been: tired, grieving, alive.

He looked across the years at her.

“Time to go,” Mara said.

Jonas nodded.

The drowned bell split from crown to lip.

Its voice broke.

Water crashed through the square without wetting it. The dead dissolved into spray. The old church folded into darkness. The harbor clock’s hands stopped at midnight.

Silence followed.

Then, one by one, the clocks began to tick.

By spring, the bell stood in the village museum, though “stood” was a generous word for three bronze fragments laid upon velvet. The mayor’s plaque described the night as an unusual atmospheric event. No one in Bellweather believed the plaque, including the mayor.

Mrs. Cale stopped claiming she had danced with the prince of Spain. She had remembered, at last, that he was Portuguese.

Elias came to the shop every Thursday. At first he brought clocks that did not need repair. Later, he stopped pretending and brought tea.

Tomas replaced the broken windows and painted a new sign.

Mara objected when she saw it.

VENN & DAUGHTER & PERHAPS REED, CLOCKS REPAIRED

“Perhaps Reed?” she said.

“I didn’t want to presume.”

“You’ve presumed an entire partnership.”

“Only perhaps.”

She made him repaint it, though she allowed him to keep a small perhaps in the lower corner.

Mr. Vale’s clock sat in the front window. The silver moon turned exactly as it should. Every day at 1:17, it paused for the length of a breath, then continued.

Mara never tried to correct it.

Sometimes, when storms came in from the east and salt rattled against the glass, all the clocks in the shop fell briefly into rhythm. Their separate ticks became one steady pulse.

On such nights, Mara would think of her father beyond the final shore, and of her mother’s unfinished song.

She no longer listened for them.

But she did not shut the window, either.
